reason: The original Music Business Worldwide article reports Suno’s statement that v6 training included user “creations” and distinguishes it from the labels’ allegations in a new complaint. It can inform piece 03 on what creators should verify about uploaded and generated work. Suno has a product and litigation stake; the labels’ claims are allegations, not findings. The article’s account of Suno’s terms does not replace checking the applicable primary terms. Repeated coverage of Suno’s statement would remain one underlying company claim.

The Italian Competition Authority’s October 6 statement identifies the Suno terms it is investigating, including unilateral changes, account termination, copyright licensing and arbitration. It can inform piece 03 about terms to verify. The authority has opened an investigation under Italian consumer law; it has made no adverse finding here. This is a direct supplemental source, not an RSS-discovered article.

WaveDisco’s author describes regenerating three self-written songs across four models with the same lyrics and prompts, then measuring LUFS and True Peak. The reported WAV–MP3 loudness gap disappeared in the two songs with format comparisons. Piece 02 can use this as a small, disclosed method test of exported-file behavior, not proof that v6 sounds better or behaves this way for all songs. The author is a Suno user with a catalog built on v5.5; this direct supplemental page does not count as RSS-discovered.

The original Los Angeles Times reporting interviews a session musician, songwriter representative, Suno adviser, union representative and others about consent and undisclosed payouts in AI licensing deals. It can inform piece 03 on questions creators should ask before relying on such deals. Speakers have differing professional and commercial stakes; the reported union and performer lawsuits remain allegations, and the article cannot establish actual payouts. This is a distinct RSS-discovered written item, even where it mentions the same Suno partnerships covered elsewhere.

MusicRadar’s original Todd Edwards interview describes his use of Suno Studio to generate material that he cuts into samples for his own productions. Piece 01 can use his account as one established producer’s workflow, with piece 02 using his distinction between prompting alone and adding musical ideas. Edwards advocates a tool he uses, and MusicRadar discloses affiliate links. His assertion that the material is entirely his and removes lawsuit risk is unverified and must not be adopted as a legal conclusion. This is a distinct RSS-discovered interview.

Suno’s October Studio release-note section specifies improved downbeat detection, shift-click-drag clip stretching, adjustable fade curves and floating plugin views. Piece 01 can report these as announced workflow changes for Premier subscribers. Suno has a direct product marketing stake; its assertions that alignment is smoother or stretching is fast are not independent performance evidence. This direct supplemental page does not count as RSS-discovered.

Dazed reports separate interviews with Kilo Kent and Zemi, who describe using Suno to change their own recorded vocals, and documents their label’s attempt to vet the article. Piece 02 can use their attributed workflow accounts and the uncertainty around what they actually contributed; piece 03 can address disclosure and identity questions. The artists and their label have a promotional stake, their histories and production claims are not independently demonstrated, and this is separate reporting rather than corroboration of Suno’s product claims.

The ytyng author describes 24 v6 generations across two songs and settings, FFT measurements on exported files, and comparison with 12 earlier tracks. Piece 02 can examine the reported spectral and dynamics measurements alongside the stated limits: different prompts and songs, different codecs, and unconfirmed earlier model versions. The author uses Suno for blog music and favors the older sound; measured spectrum cannot establish aesthetic quality. Claims that licensing caused a quality change or model retirement are inference without demonstrated causation. This direct supplemental page does not count as RSS-discovered.

The retained timestamped transcript records Josh of JG Beats Lab describing a demo-to-arrangement workflow and a song folder containing the original demo, settings, retained stems, raw vocal takes and final master (seg-00118–seg-00167). Piece 03 can cite that passage as his practitioner method. He promotes his lab and newsletter and says he works on mixes; his interpretation of Suno’s terms and ownership is not primary legal authority and needs primary-text verification before any rights statement.

The retained timestamped transcript describes the host recording two short guitar-and-vocal ideas, entering style prompts and reacting to the resulting Suno songs (seg-00016–seg-00033, seg-00039–seg-00055). Piece 02 can use this as one novice user’s account of turning rough ideas into listenable-to-him examples. His enthusiasm and artifact observations are subjective; the transcript alone does not establish audio quality, typical results or the legality of other users’ covers. It is a separate podcast episode and publisher.

The complete timestamped transcript records a creator comparing versions of one song with progressively more direction in the lyrics field, then cleaning stems and adjusting the mix in Studio (seg-00073–seg-00109, seg-00137–seg-00203, seg-00390–seg-00433). Piece 02 can discuss the demonstrated process and his reported preference; piece 01 can show a concrete Studio editing use. The creator says he does not work for Suno. The iterations, one-song sample and later mix changes cannot prove that lyric direction generally improves vocal quality, and the transcript cannot verify the sound by listening.

Andrea Olsen’s complete timestamped transcript documents uploading one of her own voice memos to Suno, specifying a 108 BPM arrangement and asking it to retain the melody, then comparing her reported result with other tools (seg-00143–seg-00221). Piece 02 can use her narrowly stated Suno workflow and reported outcome; piece 03 can use her decision to limit what she uploads (seg-00551–seg-00571). She owns Produce Like a Boss, promotes its course and provides an Instant IP referral link, so her commercial stake must be disclosed. Her copyright, training-data and competing-service claims require primary verification and cannot be treated as findings; one memo across tools with different functions is not a controlled quality ranking.
